title: Without Imagination
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from "To Build a Fire" by Jack London (1908).
body: The man flung a look back along the way he had come. The Yukon lay a mile wide and hidden under three feet of ice. On top of this ice were as many feet of snow. It was all pure white, rolling in gentle undulations where the ice-jams of the freeze-up had formed. North and south, as far as his eye could see, it was unbroken white, save for a dark hair-line that curved and twisted from around the spruce-covered island to the south, and that curved and twisted away into the north, where it disappeared behind another spruce-covered island.

But all this—the mysterious, far-reaching hairline trail, the absence of sun from the sky, the tremendous cold, and the strangeness and weirdness of it all—made no impression on the man. It was not because he was long used to it. He was a new-comer in the land, a chechaquo, and this was his first winter. The trouble with him was that he was without imagination. He was quick and alert in the things of life, but only in the things, and not in the significances.

Fifty degrees below zero meant eighty odd degrees of frost. Such fact impressed him as being cold and uncomfortable, and that was all. It did not lead him to meditate upon his frailty as a creature of temperature, and upon man's frailty in general, able only to live within certain narrow limits of heat and cold. Fifty degrees below zero stood for a bite of frost that hurt and that must be guarded against by the use of mittens, ear-flaps, warm moccasins, and thick socks. Fifty degrees below zero was to him just precisely fifty degrees below zero. That there should be anything more to it than that was a thought that never entered his head.

Per the passage, what word does the narrator use for a newcomer to the land, like the man?
According to the passage, what was the trouble with the man, according to the narrator?
options: He did not know how to build a fire

questions.prompt: Per the passage, how many degrees of frost did fifty degrees below zero mean?
Based on the passage, why did the strangeness and weirdness of the landscape make no impression on the man?
options: Not because he was used to it, but because he lacked the imagination to grasp its deeper significance
Because he had studied the landscape for many years
Because the landscape was actually quite ordinary
Because he was too tired to notice anything

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does it mean that the man was "quick and alert in the things of life, but only in the things, and not in the significances"?
options: He could notice and react to physical facts but failed to reflect on their deeper meaning
He was slow to react to anything happening around him
He understood deep philosophical ideas but ignored practical matters
He was skilled at storytelling but poor at physical tasks

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why didn't the extreme cold lead the man to think about human mortality or "man's frailty in general"?
options: He interpreted the cold only as a physical discomfort to guard against, never as something worth deeper reflection
He had already thought deeply about mortality before this journey
The cold was not actually severe enough to prompt such thoughts
He believed mortality was not affected by temperature

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the narrator emphasize that fifty degrees below zero was to the man "just precisely fifty degrees below zero"?
options: To show how literally and narrowly the man understood his surroundings, missing any larger meaning
To prove that the man was an expert in measuring temperature
To suggest that the man was exaggerating the cold
To show that the man wanted to become a scientist

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: The man's lack of imagination kept him from grasping the deeper danger and meaning of the vast, cold wilderness around him
The man was an experienced traveler who understood every danger of the Yukon
The landscape held no real dangers for a careful traveler
The man was eager to learn about the natural world around him

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the snow lay in "gentle undulations"?
According to the passage, what shape did the trail form as it crossed the snow?
options: A dark hair-line that curved and twisted

questions.prompt: Per the passage, around what kind of landscape features did the trail curve?
According to the passage, what must be guarded against with mittens, ear-flaps, moccasins, and thick socks?
options: The bite of frost from fifty degrees below zero

questions.prompt: Per the passage, was this the man's first winter in the land?
Based on the passage, why does the narrator mention that the man was "quick and alert" at all, despite lacking imagination?
options: To show his practical competence with immediate physical facts, even though he failed to grasp their larger meaning
To prove that imagination was not actually useful in the wilderness
To suggest that quickness always comes at the cost of imagination
To argue that the man was secretly very thoughtful

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes the passage's description of the landscape?
options: A vast, white, frozen wilderness broken only by a faint trail stretching far to the north and south
A small, cramped valley surrounded by mountains
A busy trading post filled with other travelers
A landscape recently transformed by a forest fire

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the man failed to consider "the significances" of things?
options: Their deeper meaning or importance beyond the immediate, physical fact
